package_info.why_malicious: The package is part of a coordinated, large-scale spam campaign targeting the Tea protocol's reward system. Thousands of nearly identical, non-functional or minimally functional npm packages are published under random names, each with artificial dependency networks, to inflate 'teaRank' and farm cryptocurrency rewards. This activity pollutes the npm ecosystem, increases the risk of accidental dependency on malicious or useless code, and undermines trust in open source software.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At publish-time, the package.json file declares thousands of dependencies on other spam packages from the same campaign, creating a dense, artificial dependency graph to manipulate the Tea protocol's ranking algorithm and maximize protocol rewards.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate npm packages almost never declare thousands of dependencies, especially on other obscure or non-functional packages. This pattern is a strong indicator of ecosystem manipulation and reward farming.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages declare only the dependencies required for their actual functionality. Here, dependencies are used solely to manipulate ranking algorithms and do not serve any technical purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some large meta-packages or frameworks may have many dependencies, but not in a random, interconnected, and non-functional manner as seen here.
key_indicators: package.json with thousands of dependencies, most of which are obscure or low-quality
Dependencies form a dense, interconnected network with other spam packages
No meaningful code or utility provided in the package

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At publish-time, the tea.yaml file is included in the repository to register the package with the Tea protocol, enabling it to participate in the reward system and receive TEA tokens.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of tea.yaml in thousands of otherwise empty or non-functional repositories is a clear indicator of automated, reward-seeking spam. The file is used to mass-register packages for protocol rewards without providing any real value.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate projects may use tea.yaml for protocol registration, but not in mass-produced, non-functional packages with no substantive code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate open source projects that genuinely use the Tea protocol for rewards and governance.
key_indicators: tea.yaml present in the root of empty or near-empty repositories
Unique codeOwner addresses for each spam package, indicating automated mass registration
No substantive code or project content accompanying the tea.yaml

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At publish-time, a minimal or meaningless README.md file is included to give the appearance of a legitimate project, but provides no documentation or utility, serving only to pass basic repository checks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: README files are expected to provide meaningful documentation. Here, they are used as filler to pass automated repository checks, with only the package name or random text and no actual information.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate projects provide substantive documentation in README.md files. In this case, the file is used solely to create the appearance of legitimacy.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Initial scaffolding for new projects may include a placeholder README, but not at this scale or with the intent to deceive.
key_indicators: README.md containing only the package name or random, meaningless text
No actual documentation, usage instructions, or project details
README.md present in thousands of similar, non-functional packages

attack_chain.action: Automated creation of thousands of fake npm packages with random names and minimal content.
attack_chain.leads_to: Mass registration of packages with the Tea protocol.

attack_chain.action: Each package declares thousands of dependencies on other spam packages, creating a dense, interconnected dependency graph.
attack_chain.leads_to: Artificial inflation of teaRank scores for all involved packages.

attack_chain.action: Each package includes a tea.yaml file to register for TEA token rewards.
attack_chain.leads_to: Eligibility for protocol rewards and further incentive to publish more spam.

attack_chain.action: Fake or minimal README files are added to pass repository checks and appear legitimate.
attack_chain.leads_to: Packages are accepted by npm and Tea protocol, completing the spam cycle.

behavioral_signatures: Packages with thousands of dependencies, especially on other obscure or low-download packages
Presence of tea.yaml in otherwise empty or non-functional repositories
Mass publication of packages with random, hyphenated names or Latin portmanteaus
Minimal or meaningless README.md files with no documentation
file_indicators: tea.yaml present in the root of the repository
package.json with an unusually high number of dependencies (hundreds or thousands)
README.md containing only the package name or random, non-informative text
network_indicators: High volume of npm publish events from the same or related accounts within a short time frame
Registration of packages with the Tea protocol (e.g., tea.xyz endpoints or mass codeOwner address submissions)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages with an abnormally high number of dependencies, especially if those dependencies are also low-quality or recently published. Flag repositories containing tea.yaml with minimal or no actual code. Detect mass publication patterns, such as many packages from the same user or with similar naming schemes. Correlate with Tea protocol registration activity (e.g., repeated codeOwner addresses or mass submissions) to identify reward-farming campaigns. Use file content analysis to flag README.md files that lack substantive documentation.
